recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — the nth term, and what cancels in the third step.

steps.label: Find the nth term
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, but never skip it — same shape as the previous question but the denominators step by 3, so both A.P.s have d = 3.

recall.must_convey: That both denominators are A.P.s with common difference 3, giving 3n − 2 and 3n + 1, so the nth term is 1/((3n−2)(3n+1)).
accept: the denominators go up by three so the nth term is one over three n minus two into three n plus one
two a p s with common difference three giving three n minus two and three n plus one
apply the a p formula to each factor
common difference three so three n minus two and three n plus one

steps.why: It is the same method as the previous question with d = 3 instead of 2 — recognising that is faster than starting from scratch.
common_mistakes: Carrying over 2n − 1 and 2n + 1 from the previous question out of habit.
Taking a = 1 for the second sequence, which starts at 4.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Both sides come to one quarter.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 both sides equal 1/4.
accept: left side is one over four and right side is one over three plus one which is a quarter
both sides are one fourth at n equals one
the first case gives a quarter each side
n equals one ki rendu sides one by four

steps.why: A single line, a full mark. The examiner is checking that the chain has a starting link.
common_mistakes: Writing 1/3 by substituting into the wrong formula.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume the statement for one value k and NUMBER the line (1) — Step 3 quotes it, so it has to be labelled.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is ASSUMED true for some k in N, written out as the sum up to k terms equals k/(3k+1), and labelled (1) for later use.
accept: assume the statement is true for k so the sum up to k terms equals k/(3k+1)
suppose s of k holds and call it equation one
take it as true for some k in the naturals and number that line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: then I assume s of k
let it be true for k

steps.why: This is the assumption the whole method rests on. It is not proved here — it is granted for ONE value, and Step 3 earns the right to pass it on.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. Identical shape to question 7: add, combine, factorise, cancel.
lines: So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That 3k² + 4k + 1 factorises as (3k+1)(k+1), the (3k+1) cancels, and (k+1)/(3k+4) is the formula at k+1 because 3k+4 = 3(k+1)+1.
accept: the numerator three k squared plus four k plus one factors as three k plus one into k plus one so three k plus one cancels
after cancelling it is k plus one over three k plus four which is the formula at k plus one
three k plus four equals three into k plus one plus one
factorise chesthe three k plus one cancel avuthundi

steps.why: The factorisation always mirrors the first denominator — here (3k+1) — which is why it cancels. That pattern is worth carrying into the exam.
common_mistakes: Not factorising the numerator, so nothing cancels.
Writing the (k+1)th denominator as (3k+2)(3k+5) instead of substituting k+1 properly.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. Write the sentence — it is one line and it is worth a full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That because S(1) is true AND S(k) implies S(k+1), the principle of mathematical induction gives the result for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k implies s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it is true for all n
hence by p m i the statement holds for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The two earlier parts prove single statements. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n, so the examiner marks the sentence that names it.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
